name: Early mountaineering
region: The Alps, the Himalaya and Britain
summary: The dress of the climber before nylon: layers of wool, silk and flannel under a windproof gabardine smock, with tweed breeches, puttees and nailed boots.

philosophy.core_thesis: Warmth comes from many thin layers, and wind is the enemy. The climber wears wool next to the skin and one tight cotton shell on top.
design_principles: Wear 4 to 6 thin layers, so that the climber can add or shed one at each rest.
Put wool or silk next to the skin, to hold heat when wet.
Close the outer smock with a deep hood and a drawcord at the hem.
Weave the outer cloth tight enough to stop a 40 km/h wind.
Cut the breeches full at the thigh and tight at the knee, over a wool puttee.
Cut the sleeve long, with a wrist cuff that closes over the glove.
Stitch the shoulder and the elbow with a double seam.
anti_patterns: A single thick coat that cannot be shed
Cotton next to the skin that holds sweat
A loose hem that lets in the wind
A coat that has no hood

silhouette.shape: A long, loose smock with a hood over many layers, tweed breeches that gather at the knee, and a puttee and a heavy boot.
silhouette.line: A hooded neck, a loose body to mid-thigh, and a tight cuff at the wrist and the knee.
silhouette.fit: Loose in the body to take the layers; close at the wrist, the knee and the ankle to keep the wind out.
silhouette.proportion: Smock to mid-thigh; breeches end at the knee; roughly 1 to 1.3 chest to hip with the layers on.
rules: Use a long hooded smock over the layers.
Seal the wrist with a close cuff and the waist with a drawcord.
Gather the breeches at the knee over a wool puttee.
Wear a wool cap or balaclava under the hood.
Carry spare wool mitts inside the smock.

fabrics.rule: Choose wool for warmth and a close cotton gabardine for wind. Tweed and flannel for the layers, silk for the inner shirt, and goose down only for the high camp.

methods: tight cotton gabardine for the outer smock
woollen layers of flannel and knit
tweed breeches with a gathered knee
eiderdown or goose down quilt for the high camp
construction.closures: Wooden toggles and a long front zip or a lace at the throat, a drawcord at the hem and a buckle at the cuff.
construction.details: A deep hood, a kangaroo pocket on the front, a leather patch at the elbow and the shoulder, and a wool puttee.

surface.pattern: Plain, and small heather checks; a Fair Isle band on the jumper.
surface.gloss: Gabardine at 3–8 GU; wool layers at 1–4 GU.
surface.wear: The smock fades and stiffens with wind and sun; the owner mends it with a patch and wears it again on the next climb.

palette.strategy: Stone, sand and heather, which hide dirt; one dark wool layer and a pale shell.

processes: weaving of tweed and flannel in the mill
knitting by hand and by machine
hand-nailing of boots by a bootmaker
making.scale: Outfitters made kit to order for each expedition; the climber also bought stock tweeds and knits from a shop.
making.signs: A hooded gabardine smock, a stack of wool layers, tweed breeches with a puttee, and a nailed leather boot.

pieces.form: Pullover hooded smock with a kangaroo pocket
Norfolk-style tweed jacket with a pleated back
Tweed breeches, tight at the knee over a puttee
Flannel shirt under a wool jumper

canonical_works.work: Windproof gabardine smock for the Everest party
Eiderdown suit for the high camp

evidence.title: George Mallory and members of the Everest expedition

emotion.target_response: A brave, spare sense of effort: the wearer looks tough, layered up and turned to the weather.

use_cases: a period costume brief for a 1920s expedition film
an image prompt for a mountain scene
a study note on layered dress
avoid_when: the brief is modern technical wear

modifiers.how: Swap the gabardine for a laminated membrane, tape the seams and cut the layers to three.
Replace the wool layers with one down-filled, box-baffled jacket.

ornament_level.note: The kit has no ornament; a Fair Isle band is the only pattern.
